evidence: The asymmetry is real and checkable in the shipped code: bash `read -r from to` puts every extra word into `to` while the JS `.filter((p) => p.length >= 2).map(([a, b]) => [a, b])` truncates to two, so one malformed line is a permanent no-op in the guard and an enforced edge in the gate. Inert only because the shipped policy file held one clean line, which is luck, not design.
guidance_note: When one data file is read by two enforcers, make both parsers reject the same shapes identically and put the malformed-line fixture in both suites, instead of asserting the agreement in a comment.

evidence: `--session-id` is a real claude flag and the original scan at claude-laws:163 tested only -p/--print and -c/--continue/-r/--resume, so a user-pinned id was joined by a minted one. The agent took the reviewer's first option and explicitly refused the second (reusing the user's id) because the pin exists to be an equality test on an id the launcher alone minted.
guidance_note: When a launcher injects a flag into someone else's argv, enumerate every host-CLI flag that collides with it before shipping the scan, not just the two that motivated it.

evidence: connect() wired no `onclose` at all, so a socket dropping mid-call left the `pending` entry unresolved forever; the module's own docblock claim that the CLI exits non-zero on error or timeout was true only for the connect-time timer. The hang defeats laws-switch's try/catch, which can only act on a rejection.
guidance_note: Enumerate every way an in-flight call can fail to settle - reply, error, close - when writing the send() wrapper, not after a reviewer names one of them.

evidence: The claim checks out: BUN_INSPECT was exported into every spawned child and inspect-eval's connect() honours arbitrary Runtime.evaluate with no token, so any local process reaching the port gets code execution inside the parent session. The agent did not fix it here but re-scoped the existing ticket's threat model and ranked it ahead of the distribution ticket; in hindsight that held, since the channel was retired outright in laws#47 before laws#48 distributed the launcher.
guidance_note: An env var carrying the address of an unauthenticated control channel is a security decision to record at the moment it is exported, not one to file later as a nuisance.

evidence: The ledger's OPEN bullet described the reload as unbuilt while the same diff shipped claude-laws (Path B) and claude-laws.test.sh exercising all four options end to end, so the doc told a maintainer to go build what the PR already contained.

evidence: `args.find((a) => !a.startsWith('--'))` genuinely picks a --summary value as the choice. evidence: The three post-relaunch exits did leave the user with no session, contradicting the file header's degrade-to-a-working-claude promise. evidence: `resume` really was dropped from the wire and re-derived downstream from a non-empty sid, even though SWITCH_ACTIONS returns it as data; the reviewer correctly noted it is unreachable through the shipped interactive flow today. evidence: Under `set -e` the three unguarded tmux goal-delivery commands sit before the mandatory retirement, so an optional step could abort the worker with the old process still live - and the iterm-worker in the same file already retires first. guidance_note: Order a mandatory step before an optional fallible one so the ordering carries the invariant, rather than guarding each fallible command as it is added.

evidence: The asymmetry is real: JS .trim() strips \r as whitespace while bash `read -r from to extra` does not treat it as an IFS separator, so a CRLF line passes the exactly-two-tokens check both sides and leaves `to` carrying a carriage return that can never match a craft name in conflicts_with(). That two-token check is exactly what F1's fix installed, so the fix that closed one divergence left a second reachable through the same lines; this is the third form of guard-and-gate disagreement in one PR.
guidance_note: Two parsers of one file diverge on whitespace their languages define differently: strip explicitly on both sides and put a CRLF fixture in both suites when the shared-parse rule is written.

evidence: Verified in git: the umbrella `[ -z "$INCOMPATIBLE" ]` check predates the PR's review rounds, but parse_edges() and per-line malformed rejection arrive with 7cb720a (F1's fix), which created a new way to reach zero edges - non-empty text, every line rejected - that the emptiness check does not cover. narrative: A 5552-line restoration PR of four separately-destroyed bodies of work ran four review rounds and 56 findings, and the agent accepted essentially all of them - no finding in this packet was pushed back on its merits. Round 2 is almost pure waste: the agent pushed a single round-1 fix (7d98fbf) while the other twelve were still being implemented, which re-triggered the reviewer against a head verified here to be an ancestor of every round-1 fix commit, so 13 of its 16 findings were stale re-reports the agent had to research and rebut one by one, two of them duplicated inside that same round. Round 3 was mostly paid for by fix incompleteness rather than new depth: eight of its twelve findings are gaps in code the review fixes had introduced or half-swept, including a port holder released only on the success path (F25 to F45), an identity check installed at the gate but not the escalation (F9 to F55), and a duplicated test block added by the F18 fix (F56). The dominant recurring shape is a fix that closes one instance of a class and leaves siblings standing - three separate guard-versus-gate divergences traced back to F1, and four copies of one stale Path-A claim traced back to F5. Where the agent did well it was by measuring rather than reasoning: it disproved the reviewer's own suggested remedy on F13, resolved the reviewer's uncertainty on F18 against the real binary, and repeatedly reported surviving mutations rather than implying coverage it did not have.
guidance_observations: A mid-round partial push re-triggered the reviewer while twelve of thirteen round-1 fixes were still in flight, buying a whole round in which 13 of 16 findings were stale.
The reviewer duplicated findings inside a single round (F31 with F39, F38 with F41), so its per-round finding count overstates the number of distinct issues.

Fixes were dispatched to implementing subagents and at least twice the subagent caught a contradiction in the posted plan and reported it rather than quietly picking one, which is what kept two wrong remedies out of the tree.

Almost every fix reply reports mutation testing, and it repeatedly caught vacuous coverage - fixtures that never presented a realistic terminal page, assertions satisfied by the runner's ambient process tree, a victim process that rewrote its own ps line.
The craft guard's refusal to let a code-craft session edit agent-facing docs turned two one-line doc corrections into tickets (F30, F47) in files this same PR had already edited during review.
The agent's plan-then-correct-in-public habit (F6, F13) surfaced two wrong plans before they landed, and cost nothing but a thread comment.
